b0: If you live in Singapore, you have breathed this smoke. What is it costing your lungs, and why does it never stop coming back? In the next few minutes, we will follow this smoke backwards, from your window to the fire that made it, and find the one point on that path where you can step in.
b1: So where does it come from? Not from Singapore. During the dry season, fires burn across parts of Sumatra and Kalimantan in Indonesia, and sometimes in Malaysia. From around June to October, the southwest monsoon winds carry that smoke across the region, straight to us. The wind is the delivery truck. It is not the cause.
b2: Here is the part most people never learn. Many of these fires are not burning in normal soil. They burn in peat. Peat is a thick layer of dead plants that has built up over thousands of years in waterlogged swamps. Because it is always wet, the plants never fully rot. They just pile up, storing huge amounts of carbon.
b3: But when companies or farmers dig canals to drain the swamp for plantations, the peat dries out. And dry peat is basically fuel. Once it catches fire, it does not just burn on the surface. It smoulders underground, sometimes metres deep, for weeks. Water bombing from helicopters barely touches it. And because it burns slowly with little oxygen, the combustion is incomplete, which is exactly the kind of burning that produces the most smoke.
